Good questions, and you're going to receive different answers depending on who you ask. I think that Python 3 is one of the better languages to start with, because not only is it relatively easy to learn from a syntax point of view, but it comes with a lot of "batteries included." What I mean is that the Python standard library has a lot of tools that are helpful for developers that you'll neither have to fuss with installing or write yourself. Things like working with files and so on. Beyond the standard library, there are lots of powerful libraries and frameworks written in Python that you can install if needed.

When it comes to the learning part, I would suggest a 2-pronged approach. Half reading a book and doing exercises, half following an online course that gives you feedback.

The book that I would recommend is "Think Python: How to Think Like a Computer Scientist." It's a free PDF. High quality.
Web page: https://greenteapress.com/wp/think-python-2e/ PDF link: http://greenteapress.com/thinkpython2/thinkpython2.pdf

The book suggests https://www.pythonanywhere.com/pricing/ as a web-based way to play around with Python without having to install it on a local machine. The beginner account is free and it's enough to start learning.

The online courses can be found in numerous places. The free account at Datacamp gives you access to 9 courses. They tend to be data analysis focused after the first introductory parts, but it's good to be doing something productive with the code like making graphs. https://www.datacamp.com/courses/tech:python

This website is powered by Datacamp and is a good tutorial: https://www.learnpython.org/

As you get deeper into the language, you'll find yourself wanting to look over the documentation written by the developers. There are two really helpful parts: The language reference (the explicit rules for parts of the language) and the library reference (the documentation on the standard library). They can be found here: https://docs.python.org/3/

The python.org site is a great resource. Here is a wiki page for a lot of online resources: https://wiki.python.org/moin/BeginnersGuide/NonProgrammers

Have fun!
